title: Fibres: Natural, Synthetic & Blended
description: Natural, synthetic and blended fibres — sources, properties, uses and their ecological and social footprint.
content_html:
Where Fibres Come From

All textiles begin with a fibre — a fine, hair-like strand that is spun into yarn and woven, knitted or bonded into fabric. Fibres fall into two broad families: natural (sourced from plants and animals) and synthetic (manufactured from chemicals, usually derived from crude oil). Understanding the origin of each fibre is essential because it directly determines the fibre's properties and its environmental impact.

Natural Fibres

Cotton is a cellulose fibre harvested from the seed pod of the cotton plant, grown in warm climates such as India, the USA and China. It is soft, comfortable against the skin, strong when wet and highly absorbent — making it ideal for T-shirts, towels and bed linen. Cotton is breathable but creases easily and can shrink if washed at high temperatures.

Wool is a protein fibre shorn from sheep (and other animals such as alpacas and goats for specialist wools). It is naturally warm because the crimped fibre traps air pockets, and it has excellent moisture management — absorbing up to 30% of its own weight in water vapour without feeling wet. Wool is used for knitwear, suits and blankets. It requires careful washing because it felts if agitated in hot water.

Silk is a continuous protein filament produced by the silkworm (Bombyx mori) as it spins its cocoon. Silk is exceptionally smooth, lustrous and strong for its weight. It drapes beautifully and is used for luxury garments, scarves and linings. Silk is expensive because production is labour-intensive: the cocoons must be unreeled by hand in hot water to preserve the continuous filament.

Linen is made from the stem fibres of the flax plant. It is one of the oldest textile fibres known to humanity. Linen is stronger than cotton, highly absorbent, and becomes softer and more lustrous with washing. It is cool to wear in summer but creases severely. Linen is used for shirts, trousers, table linen and home furnishings.

Key Fact

Natural plant fibres (cotton, linen) are made of cellulose; natural animal fibres (wool, silk) are made of protein. This distinction matters: cellulose fibres generally absorb moisture well, while protein fibres naturally resist fire and can absorb moisture vapour without feeling damp.

Synthetic Fibres

Synthetic fibres are manufactured by extruding a liquid polymer through tiny holes called spinnerets to produce continuous filaments. The raw material is almost always derived from crude oil, a non-renewable petrochemical resource.

Polyester is the world's most widely produced synthetic fibre. It is strong, durable, wrinkle-resistant and dries very quickly — properties that make it ideal for sportswear, fleece jackets and workwear. Polyester does not absorb moisture well, which can make it feel clammy next to the skin during exercise, though modern microfibre versions draw sweat away by capillary action.

Nylon (polyamide) was the first fully synthetic fibre, developed in the 1930s. It is exceptionally strong and abrasion-resistant, making it popular for tights, hosiery, ropes, parachutes and backpack fabrics. Nylon is lightweight and recovers well from stretching, but like polyester it absorbs little moisture and can build up static charge.

Acrylic is often used as a cheaper substitute for wool because it is soft, lightweight and warm. Acrylic is resistant to sunlight degradation, making it useful for outdoor fabrics and upholstery. However, it pills readily (small balls of fibre form on the surface), it melts rather than burns and it is not biodegradable.

Elastane (brand name Lycra) is a polyurethane-based fibre capable of stretching to five to seven times its original length and recovering fully (some sources cite up to 8×; 5–6× is the most commonly cited figure) and recovering fully. Even a small percentage added to a fabric (2–5%) gives it significant stretch and recovery. Elastane is used in swimwear, cycling shorts, sportswear and stretch denim.

The manufacturing process is called melt spinning (for polyester and nylon) or wet spinning (for acrylic). In melt spinning, the polymer chips are melted and forced through a spinneret. The fine streams of polymer solidify in cool air to form continuous filaments, which are then drawn (stretched) under tension to align the polymer chains — this increases strength and reduces extensibility. Multiple filaments are bundled into a yarn. Filament yarns are smooth and lustrous; filaments can also be cut into short lengths called staple fibres to mimic the texture of natural fibres when spun.

Blended and Mixed Fibres

A blended fibre combines two or more fibre types in the same yarn to combine the best properties of each. The most common example is polycotton (typically 65% polyester, 35% cotton): polyester contributes durability, quick drying and wrinkle resistance; cotton contributes softness, breathability and comfort. Polycotton is used for school shirts, bed sheets and workwear.

A mixed fabric uses different fibres in the warp and weft yarns (the threads running lengthways and widthways in a woven fabric) rather than blending them in the same yarn. The result is a fabric with different properties in each direction. Blending and mixing allow designers to engineer performance characteristics that no single fibre could provide alone.

Key Fact

Blends are created to improve performance (e.g. stretch + strength), reduce cost (synthetic fibres are cheaper than silk or wool), and balance care requirements (machine-washable wool blends are easier to maintain than 100% wool). Always link each fibre in the blend to a specific benefit it contributes.

Ecological and Social Footprint of Fibre Production

No fibre is entirely without environmental or social impact. Cotton is the world's most pesticide-intensive crop — conventional cotton production uses roughly 6% of the world's pesticides despite occupying only 2.4% of its farmland. It also requires enormous volumes of water: it takes approximately 10,000 litres of water to produce 1 kilogram of cotton. Organic cotton avoids synthetic pesticides but yields less per hectare and is more expensive.

Synthetic fibres such as polyester and nylon depend on crude oil, a finite, non-renewable resource. Their production involves energy-intensive chemical processes and releases greenhouse gases. Crucially, synthetic fabrics shed microplastics — tiny plastic fragments — every time they are washed. These particles pass through wastewater treatment systems into rivers and oceans, entering the food chain. A single wash of a fleece jacket can release more than 700,000 microplastic fibres.

The social footprint of fibre production includes working conditions in cotton-farming communities (where pesticide exposure causes health problems), and in textile mills where low wages, long hours and poor safety standards remain common concerns in some producing countries. Fair trade certification schemes and industry codes of conduct aim to improve conditions, but enforcement is patchy across global supply chains.

One response to the environmental cost of virgin synthetic fibre is recycled polyester (rPET), made by melting down plastic bottles or post-consumer textile waste and extruding new filaments. Producing rPET uses approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester. Many sportswear brands now use rPET extensively in their ranges. However, recycled synthetics still shed microplastics, and the sorting, cleaning and reprocessing of mixed-fibre garments remains technically challenging, so not all post-consumer textile waste can currently be recycled back into fibre.
exam_tip_html: Fibre questions often ask you to 'justify' or 'evaluate' a material choice — simply naming a property earns 1 mark, but explaining why that property is an advantage for the specific product and user earns the higher marks. For example: 'Polyester is used because it is quick-drying (property), which means a sports top remains comfortable during exercise and dries between training sessions (application).' On 6- and 8-mark questions, also consider disadvantages or environmental trade-offs to demonstrate balanced evaluation.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Natural fibres (cotton, wool, silk, linen) come from plant or animal sources; synthetic fibres (polyester, nylon, acrylic, elastane) are manufactured from crude oil polymers extruded through spinnerets.
  • Blended fibres combine two or more fibre types in the same yarn to balance properties such as comfort, strength, cost and ease of care; polycotton is the most common example.
  • All fibre production carries an ecological and social footprint — cotton is pesticide- and water-intensive; synthetic fibres depend on finite oil and shed microplastics; fair trade and recycled synthetics are partial responses.

glossary_terms.definition: The raw, hair-like strand that forms the basic unit of all textile materials; fibres are spun into yarns and then made into fabric.
A metal plate with tiny holes through which liquid polymer is forced to produce continuous synthetic filaments; the filaments harden on contact with air or water.
A fabric made by combining two or more different fibre types during the spinning of the yarn, so both fibres are intimately mixed in each thread.
Tiny plastic fragments shed by synthetic fabrics during washing that pass into waterways and enter the food chain.

practice_questions.text:
Which fibre is produced by extruding a liquid polymer through spinnerets?
A) Cotton
B) Linen
C) Polyester
D) Wool
Name two natural animal fibres used in textile production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: wool, silk, cashmere, alpaca. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe three properties of cotton that make it suitable for T-shirts.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• Cotton is soft and comfortable against the skin.
• It is highly absorbent, drawing perspiration away from the body.
• It is breathable, allowing air to circulate and helping to regulate body temperature. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why polycotton (65% polyester / 35% cotton) is used for school shirts rather than 100% cotton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The polyester content makes the fabric more durable and resistant to wear, extending the garment's life.
• Polyester dries quickly after washing and resists creasing, reducing ironing time for parents.
• The cotton content retains breathability and softness, keeping the shirt comfortable to wear all day.
• Blending reduces material cost compared to 100% cotton, making the garment more affordable.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the environmental concerns associated with the production of synthetic fibres and evaluate one strategy manufacturers use to reduce this impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Synthetic fibres such as polyester and nylon are derived from crude oil, a finite non-renewable resource, so their production depletes fossil fuel reserves.
• Manufacturing processes are energy-intensive and release greenhouse gases, contributing to climate change.
• Each wash of a synthetic garment releases hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres that enter waterways and the food chain, harming aquatic ecosystems.
• Strategy: recycled polyester (rPET) is made by reprocessing plastic bottles or post-consumer textile waste, using approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester.
• Limitation: rPET still sheds microplastics, and sorting mixed-fibre garments for recycling remains technically difficult, so impact is reduced but not eliminated.
[6 marks — Mastering: Two environmental concerns explained fully plus strategy evaluated with limitation. Secure: Two concerns and strategy named but limited evaluation. Developing: One concern explained; strategy mentioned superficially. Emerging: Partial or vague points.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using natural fibres compared with synthetic fibres for a sportswear manufacturer designing performance running kit.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of natural fibres for running kit:
• Merino wool is naturally moisture-wicking and odour-resistant (wool fibre structure absorbs vapour but wicks liquid), reducing unpleasant smells during extended runs.
• Natural fibres are generally more biodegradable at end of life, reducing landfill impact.
Disadvantages of natural fibres for running kit:
• Wool and cotton are heavier than synthetic equivalents when dry, and significantly heavier when wet, affecting performance.
• Natural fibres are typically more expensive and can take longer to dry than synthetics such as polyester.
Advantages of synthetics for running kit:
• Polyester is lightweight, durable and quick-drying; adding elastane provides stretch and close fit without restricting movement.
• Synthetics can be engineered to specific performance specifications (e.g. reflective yarns, UV protection) that natural fibres cannot match.
Disadvantages of synthetics for running kit:
• Synthetics absorb little moisture and can feel clammy; they also retain odour-causing bacteria more readily than natural fibres.
• Microplastic shedding from synthetic sportswear during washing is an environmental harm that many consumers now consider.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained balanced discussion, at least two developed points per side linked specifically to running kit context. Secure: Points identified with some development, reasonable balance. Developing: Listed points, limited development, imbalanced. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which fibre is a continuous protein filament produced by the silkworm?
Which synthetic fibre can stretch up to eight times its original length and recover fully?
Cotton is a _____ fibre harvested from the seed pod of the cotton plant.
Polycotton is a _____ fibre, combining polyester and cotton in the same yarn.
Match each fibre to its correct source or key property:
right: Protein fibre shorn from sheep; warm and moisture-managing
Derived from crude oil; strong, quick-drying and wrinkle-resistant
Cellulose fibre from the stem of the flax plant; cool and strong

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a natural fibre and a synthetic fibre?
flashcard_questions.a: Natural fibres come from plants or animals; synthetic fibres are manufactured from crude oil polymers.

flashcard_questions.q: Which plant does cotton fibre come from?
flashcard_questions.a: The seed pod of the cotton plant, grown in warm climates.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is wool described as a warm fibre?
flashcard_questions.a: Its crimped structure traps air pockets, providing natural insulation.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes silk exceptionally expensive compared with cotton?
flashcard_questions.a: Production is labour-intensive — cocoons must be unreeled by hand to preserve the continuous filament.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the chemical structure shared by cotton and linen.
flashcard_questions.a: Both are cellulose fibres derived from plant cell walls.

flashcard_questions.q: What are spinnerets used for in synthetic fibre production?
flashcard_questions.a: Metal plates with tiny holes through which liquid polymer is forced to form continuous filaments.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two properties that make polyester suitable for sportswear.
flashcard_questions.a: Strong and durable; quick-drying and wrinkle-resistant.

flashcard_questions.q: What is elastane, and what percentage is typically added to a fabric to give stretch?
flashcard_questions.a: A polyurethane fibre; as little as 2-5% gives significant stretch and recovery.
Two or more fibre types combined within the same yarn to balance their properties.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is polycotton used for school shirts rather than 100% polyester?
flashcard_questions.a: Cotton content adds breathability and softness; polyester adds durability and easy care.

flashcard_questions.q: What environmental problem is caused by washing synthetic fabrics?
flashcard_questions.a: Microplastic fibres are shed and pass into waterways, entering the food chain.

flashcard_questions.q: How does recycled polyester (rPET) reduce environmental impact compared with virgin polyester?
flashcard_questions.a: It is made from waste plastic bottles and uses approximately 59% less energy to produce.
